counterfactual_missing_items: no parkinsonism is mentioned, which would be needed to strengthen DLB
no acute/fluctuating onset over hours-days; there are three months of progressive decline, arguing against delirium
no myoclonus, ataxia, or typical CJD EEG/MRI pattern
response.rationale: R2 is strongly supported by pathognomonic catatonic motor signs (echopraxia, mitmachen, mutism, staring) and withdrawal, with no contradictory raw data. R7 is the runner-up because it accounts for progressive dementia, visual hallucinations, and fluctuating cognition, but it lacks parkinsonism and does not explain the catatonia signs. R6 captures inattention and EEG slowing but is disfavored by the three-month course and lack of an acute toxic/metabolic trigger. R4/R8 rely on nonspecific white-matter ischemia; R1/R5/R9 are contradicted by high B12, normal TSH, and negative RPR; R10 lacks typical CJD features; R3 is an unlikely drug mechanism and cannot explain the motor syndrome.

rejected.why: B12 is high, not low, and homocysteine 12.3 is not deficiency-level.
Mirtazapine psychosis has no clear temporal causality and does not explain echopraxia/mitmachen/mutism.
Chronic ischemic encephalopathy is a nonspecific restatement of white-matter ischemia and does not account for hallucinations/catatonia.
TSH is normal, directly contradicting active hypothyroid encephalopathy.
Delirium is unlikely with a 3-month progressive course and no acute metabolic/toxic precipitant; it also misses the catatonic motor signs.
Vascular dementia is supported only by nonspecific white-matter changes and lacks stepwise/focal deficits; no acute infarcts are described.
Serum RPR is negative, excluding neurosyphilis.
CJD lacks myoclonus, ataxia, typical MRI/EEG changes, and has only nonspecific progressive decline/hallucinations.
